Letter to the Editor
In stroke patients, lower LDL-cholesterol is actually better
Dear Editor,
Internists often treat patients with dyslipidemia or atherosclerotic
cardiovascular disease (ASCVD); however, there remain questions re-
garding what degree of reduction in low density lipoprotein cholesterol
(LDL-C) is suﬃcient, and what supporting evidence there is for this.
Studies have consistently shown that coronary heart disease (CHD)
risk is correlated closely with LDL-C levels, and that the lower the LCL-
C, the lower the CHD and cardiovascular (CV) risk [1]. Over 15 years
ago, in the landmark studies PROVE IT-TIMI 22 and TNT, the beneﬁts
of aggressive lipid-lowering interventions were seen in patients ex-
periencing an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) event and in stable CHD
patients, respectively [2,3].
In 2004, the Adult Treatment Panel (ATP)
III was updated to embrace the ﬁndings from several trials, and re-
commended that physicians consider altering their LDL-C treatment
goals from less than 100 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) to less than 70 mg/dL
(1.8 mmol/L) for certain patients at very high risk for future CHD
events [4].
In contrast, the target level for LDL-C to reduce CV events after
stroke has not been well established. In fact, the recently published
guidelines
of
the
European
Society
of
Cardiology/European
Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) and the current guidelines of the
American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA)
recommend statin therapy with intensive lipid-lowering eﬀects after an
ischemic stroke or Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) presumed to be of
atherosclerotic origin, but do not stipulate a target level of LDL-C be-
cause there is limited data on outcomes with diﬀerent targets for LDL-C
[1,5].
A sub-analysis of the data from the Stroke Prevention by Aggressive
Reduction in Cholesterol Level (SPARCL) trial (the ﬁrst trial to speci-
ﬁcally look at the eﬀect of a statin, speciﬁcally atorvastatin, in patients
with a prior stroke or TIA but with no history of elevated cholesterol or
CHD) has shown that patients who reached a level of LDL-C of less than
70 mg/dl (1.8 mmol per liter) had a 28% lower relative risk of stroke
than those who reached a level of 100 mg per deciliter (2.6 mmol per
liter) [6]. A further meta-regression analysis, including results from the
SPARCL trial, has also shown that the risk of stroke was 20% lower for
every reduction of 39 mg /dl (1.0 mmol per liter) in the LDL-C level,
without any threshold eﬀect [7].
With the recent publication of the Treat Stroke to Target trial [8],
the landscape has ﬁnally changed. For the ﬁrst time a study has shown
that prescribing lipid-lowering therapy to achieve a more aggressive
LDL-C treatment target in patients who have had a TIA or ischemic
stroke of atherosclerotic origin reduces the risk of major CV events. In
this parallel-group trial conducted in France and South Korea, patients
who had suﬀered an ischemic stroke in the previous 3 months or a TIA
within the previous 15 days were randomly assigned to a target LDL-C
level of less than 70 mg per deciliter (1.8 mmol per liter) (lower-target
group), or to a target range of 90 mg to 110 mg per deciliter (2.3 to
2.8 mmol per liter) (higher-target group). All the patients had evidence
of cerebrovascular or coronary-artery atherosclerosis and received a
statin, ezetimibe, or both.
A total of 2860 patients were enrolled and followed for a median of
3.5 years. Though the study was stopped prematurely due to a funding
shortfall, at follow-up, the primary composite outcome - of ischemic
stroke, myocardial infarction, new symptoms leading to urgent cor-
onary or carotid revascularization, or death from CV causes - had oc-
curred in 8.5% of patients in the lower-target group, and in 10.9% of
patients with the more moderate LDL-C goal, representing a 22% re-
lative
risk
reduction
(Hazard
Ratio
0.78;
95%
CI
0.61–0.98).
Importantly, the incidence of intracranial hemorrhage —a key concern
for aggressive LDL-C lowering in these patients—was not increased in
patients in the lower-target group.
However, we must also take into account that in the real-world
setting, many studies have shown that a relatively high proportion of
patients fail to achieve the recommended LDL-C objective. On one
hand, patients with cerebrovascular disease are signiﬁcantly less likely
to receive a higher intensity statin or achieve LDL-C <100 mg/dl than
patients with CHD [9]; on the other, even in a Stroke Prevention Clinic,
less than 50% of patients achieve their LDL-C cholesterol target, espe-
cially diabetic patients [10].
Therefore, though the general principle of “the lower, the better” for
LDL-C can now be fully applied to patients with ischemic stroke or TIA
to prevent ASCVD, future eﬀorts are needed to promote optimal use of
lipid-lowering therapy in these patients. The change is in our hands.
Declaration of competing interest
None.
